paras: The beating of Arthur Patterson and William Black was an attack by a crowd of white men on two Black men on the West Side of New York City on November 3, 1903, after a sixteen-year-old white boy, Jeremiah Healy, was shot in the street. Both men were beaten so badly that they were taken to Roosevelt Hospital, and the papers reported that only the arrival of police kept them from being killed. Patterson, charged with the shooting, denied it, and the attack was reported in two New York dailies and by wire across the country.

Healy lived at No. 776 Tenth avenue; Patterson, given as twenty-eight by the Evening World and twenty-five by the Sun, lived at No. 205 West Sixty-first street. William Black, twenty-seven, lived at No. 231 West Sixty-eighth street. The shooting took place around noon, in Sixty-eighth street according to the Evening World and at Sixtieth street and Amsterdam avenue according to the Sun.

Healy told the Evening World that he was passing through Sixty-eighth street when Patterson fired five shots from a hallway, one of which struck him in the right leg. Policeman Thomas Brady of the West Sixty-eighth street station gave the Sun a different account, in which the boy was playing in the street when Patterson approached and, "for no known reason," fired five shots, one hitting him in the groin. Black, who was in the street at the time, was "mistaken by some of the passers by" for the man who had fired.

A crowd of about 500 chased the two men to Tenth avenue, where it set on them with clubs and kicked them. Brady said Patterson had fled home, over the roof and back to Amsterdam avenue, where the crowd threw him down and beat him "unmercifully." Patrolmen Byrne and Brady drove the crowd back, and Brady later said he thought the crowd would have killed Patterson had he not appeared. A rubbish fire near the gas tank at Fifty-fifth street and Amsterdam avenue then drew off the crowd's attention.

The two men could hardly stand at the station house and were sent to Roosevelt Hospital, as was Healy. The Evening World and the wire called Healy's wound not serious, while the Sun reported that at the hospital his condition was said to be critical.

After their wounds were dressed, both men were taken to the West Side Court, Patterson charged with the shooting and Black arrested on suspicion. Before Magistrate Flammer, Patterson said he was afraid for his life and denied the shooting, saying he had been in a nearby restaurant and that the crowd pounced on him when he went out to look. He was held without bail for further examination. The Sun did not mention Black, and no report of the outcome of either case, or of any arrest of members of the crowd, was found.

The Evening World's headline, "Crowd Beats Man Who Shot Boy," stated Patterson's guilt as fact, although its text said only that he was "accused" and that Black had been mistaken for the shooter. The Sun, under "Crowd Attacks a Negro," was the only paper to print Patterson's denial.

A wire dispatch dated November 3 described the victims as "negroes" suspected of shooting "a white boy," set upon by a mob of five hundred white men, and said that "the arrival of two policemen saved them from being killed." It ran that day in the Washington Evening Star and on November 4 in papers from Montgomery to Saint Paul, under headlines such as "Negroes Are Beaten" and "Negroes Almost Killed by Mob." The Portland Daily Press and the Breathitt County News placed it among reports of election-day shootings and stabbings. Weekly papers in North Dakota and Wisconsin were still carrying a one-line version, saying the two men were "beaten almost to death," as late as November 13.
All of the coverage found came from white papers; no report of the attack was found in the Black press.
Every account of the shooting came from Healy or the police and they differed on how it happened and on Black's part in it, while Patterson, the only other source, denied firing at all.

reader.title: Beating of Arthur Patterson and William Black
bases: A crowd of white men chased and beat two Black men suspected of shooting a white boy until police intervened; neither man was killed (A1, A2, A3).
Two independent New York dailies (A1, A3) and the wire dispatch (A2) agree that a crowd beat Patterson after Healy was shot and that police rescued him.

accounts.gist: Healy said he was passing through Sixty-eighth street when Patterson fired five shots from a hallway, one hitting his right leg; Black was mistaken by passers-by for the shooter.

accounts.label: Policeman Brady's account (Sun)
accounts.gist: The boy was playing at Sixtieth street and Amsterdam avenue when Patterson approached and fired five shots at him for no known reason, then fled home, over the roof and back to Amsterdam avenue, where the crowd beat him until Brady rescued him.

accounts.label: Patterson's account (in court)
accounts.gist: He was in a nearby restaurant when he heard shots, went out to see what had happened, and the crowd pounced on him; he had nothing to do with the shooting.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Patterson and Black, suspected of shooting a white boy, were set upon by a mob of 500 white men and beaten so badly they were hospitalized; two policemen saved them from being killed.

framing.detail: The Evening World headlined 'Crowd Beats Man Who Shot Boy', stating the accusation as fact, though the text says Patterson was 'accused' and Black 'mistaken'.
The Sun headlined 'Crowd Attacks a Negro' and printed both Brady's account and Patterson's denial.

The wire dispatch stressed race on both sides ('negroes', 'a white boy', 'five hundred white men') and ran under headlines such as 'Negroes Are Beaten' and 'Negroes Almost Killed by Mob', often in columns of election-day violence.
